overview: The Duchy of Parma and Piacenza was a northern Italian state ruled by several dynasties. The map’s 1650 to 1815 interval hides French administration beginning in 1802 and formal imperial incorporation in 1808. A restored duchy continued after Napoleon, well beyond 1815. The outline is approximate, rather than a precise border across these political changes.

periods.title: Dynastic government
periods.summary: Farnese, Bourbon and Austrian rulers governed in successive phases.

periods.title: French administration
periods.summary: French administration led to incorporation in the imperial Taro department in 1808.

periods.title: Restored ducal government
periods.summary: Restoration brought new rulers before the final political upheaval of 1859.

items.text: French rule developed in stages. After Duke Ferdinando died in 1802, an administrator governed in Napoleon’s name. Conscription and the Napoleonic civil code followed in 1805, and the Taro department was formally created in 1808. Such changes affected military service, laws and the language of official documents.

After Napoleon’s fall, restoring government required rebuilding the duchy’s finances and administration. Minister Filippo Magawly directed that work from 1814. Maria Luigia, formerly empress of the French, reached Parma on 20 April 1816 to govern the duchy assigned to her. Her arrival falls just beyond the imported map interval.

sections.title: Schools, books and the problem of finding a book

items.text: The 1768 educational constitutions reorganized instruction from primary schooling to the university. Parma’s reforming government supported institutions including a botanical garden, an antiquities museum and a public library. These projects helped train professionals and collect knowledge, although a law about education does not tell us that every child could attend.

Parma’s first chemistry chair was established within medicine in 1767. The following year, the former Jesuit complex of San Rocco became the ducal university’s home after the Jesuits were expelled. Scientific education was growing, but changes to teaching institutions could also involve forceful political and religious conflict.

The Palatina Library began as a public-benefit project in 1761 and was officially inaugurated in 1769. Librarian Paolo Maria Paciaudi assembled thousands of books through purchases and scholarly contacts. Building a library meant finding the books first, not merely building beautiful shelves.

Paciaudi recorded books on movable catalogue slips instead of only in a bound register. The slips included an author, title, publication details, comments and the book’s location. A new acquisition could get a new slip without requiring a librarian to rewrite a whole book of entries.

Giambattista Bodoni arrived in 1768 to establish and direct the royal printing shop. He supervised the making of presses and tools, with both the workshop and his lodgings inside the Pilotta complex. Producing elegant pages depended on practical labor, from preparing equipment to arranging and printing the type.

Writing sample: a 1769 festival book begins its Italian title “Descrizione delle feste celebrate in Parma l’anno MDCCLXIX.” This means, “Description of the festivities celebrated in Parma in the year 1769.” The museum transcribes the title of Bodoni’s book for Duke Ferdinando’s wedding to Maria Amalia. The Roman numerals spell out the year.

Bodoni’s widow, Margherita Dall’Aglio, continued running the printing shop after his death. In 1818 she published his great typographic manual in two volumes. It displayed letterforms and decorative designs accumulated over his career. This achievement belongs to the restored duchy, after the map’s cutoff, and depended on her continuing the work.

sections.title: Food, a walk and care for children

items.text: Before this map interval, an official document of 1612 specified places whose cheese could be sold as Parmigiano. It named dairying areas around Parma, including Fontevivo and Noceto. Protecting a food’s geographical reputation was already serious business, although this early rule was not the same system as today’s protected designation.

Parma’s new promenade and coffee pavilion opened on 24 June 1766. The regional heritage catalogue connects that evening with the local custom of walking outdoors in the Saint John festivities to encounter the dew. A stroll could combine fresh air, company and a fashionable new place to pause.

During the eighteenth century, Parma’s old hospital was divided into the Misericordia section for care of the sick and injured and the Esposti section for foundlings. Assistance to children without parental care therefore formed part of this large institution’s responsibilities, alongside treating illness.

The Farnese Theatre was a place for exceptional court celebrations rather than an everyday evening out. Its elaborate productions were so costly that it was used only nine times, from its opening in 1628 to the last dynastic event in 1732. Even dukes could build a stage that was expensive to keep busy.

ending.text: Ducal rule collapsed in 1859. Duchess Luisa Maria left Parma in June, Austrian troops withdrew from Piacenza, and provisional authorities pursued union with Sardinia. The territories entered the process of Italian unification. The imported ending in 1815 instead falls near the beginning of the restored duchy.
